[13] The appellants have viable IFAs in Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai, and Indore. As defined in Ranganathan v. Canada, an IFA is viable if 1) the appellants do not face s. 97 harm or a reasonable chance of persecution there, and 2) conditions in the IFA are such that it would not be unreasonable for the appellants to seek refuge there.9
First prong of the IFA test: Risk of persecution or s. 97 harm

[14] The appellants have not established on a balance of probabilities that the agents of harm are motivated to pursue them in the IFA locations such that they would face a reasonable chance of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, s. 97 harm there.
The agents of harm are not sufficiently motivated to pursue the appellants in the IFAs

[15] The RPD was correct that the appellants have not established that the police officers who are the agents of harm in this case are motivated to pursue them in the IFAs. While I accept that the police have visited the appellants' family and friends in their home state, and that this demonstrates that they have a continuing interest in the appellants, the appellants have not established that the police are motivated to take steps to track the appellants if they were residing in one of the IFAs elsewhere in the country.10 The primary reasons for reaching this conclusion are that it appears that police interest in the appellants has been extrajudicial and unofficial and that this is not the type of case in which police are motivated to cooperate in a multi-state manhunt.11 The objective documentary evidence indicates that police in different jurisdictions cooperate on major crimes.12 There is insufficient evidence before me that state police cooperate with police in other states to persecute individuals who have been pursued by local police and released upon payment of bribes without being charged with any crime.13

[16] This is not a case where the appellants have established that the police genuinely view them as militants or anti-nationals.14 Instead, the statements attributed to the authorities throughout the Basis of Claim narrative indicate that the agents of harm have accused the principal appellant of having information about militants from having worked at the same company as a suspected militant, or of having helped militants by, say, working with the family of a suspected one to make what the authorities described as a "false police complaint", but not of actually being a militant.15 As such, I conclude that the authorities are not motivated to pursue the appellants because they suspect them of being militant anti-nationals.

When considering their risk as a result of such events, I place the most weight on the letter from the Indian lawyer who spoke with these appellants, who states that other people wanted to file a case, however this lawyer advised that they could only proceed with the case if the appellants offered to be witnesses, something that "they were unable to do".17 I am not satisfied that such discussions about a legal case mean that the agents of harm are motivated to pursue the appellants in the IFA locations.

[18] Like the RPD, I find that the appellants have not credibly established on a balance of probabilities that the Punjab police have pursued them elsewhere in India. The appellants write in their narrative that the police did so, with the principal appellant stating that in XXXX 2019, police raided at Delhi for his wife because she had not reported to them, as expected. However, when the RPD asked questions about this alleged presence of the agents of harm in Delhi, in order to test the credibility of the allegation, the appellants offered shifting and inconsistent testimony. Specifically, a) at the hearing the principal appellant testified that there was a completely separate police raid in Delhi years prior that is not mentioned in the Basis of Claim narrative the appellants swore was complete, and b) the appellants provided inconsistent evidence about whether police raided their family member's home within four days of the principal appellant's arrival in 2017, causing him to flee at that point,18 or whether the principal appellant remained in that home for weeks19 and the police raid only occurred subsequent to his departure from India.20 These omissions and inconsistencies were not reasonably explained and, when asked to explain why their family member's affidavit does not mention multiple alleged police raids to his home, the principal appellant suggested that the family member lied or gave false evidence in the affidavit that the appellant provided to this Board.21

[19] The appellants do not dispute these credibility conclusions on appeal and I independently find that they are correct. The omission of the alleged police raid in Delhi is not reasonably explained as the appellants included less important events in their narrative, as the RPD noted. The appellants' testimony that they think that their family member may have given false evidence in the affidavit that they submitted to the Board does not reasonably explain the discrepancies identified by the RPD. Findings of credibility may be made on the basis that the witness failed to tender important evidence at an earlier opportunity, thus bringing into question whether it is a recent fabrication.22 Statements in support of a claim have to be accurate else the inaccuracies can be held against a claimant.23 The appellants do not submit that this evidence was affected by trauma or the other issues discussed in section 7 of this Board's gender guidelines.

[20] I conclude that the appellants' evidence about the agents of harm searching for them in Delhi is not credible and trustworthy. They have not established on a balance of probabilities that any such raids have occurred. That said, while I draw an adverse inference about the credibility of the appellants' evidence on this one point, this is not a case in which I conclude that the appellants are generally not credible or that their allegations regarding events in Punjab state are not credible.
Lack of motivation is determinative of the first prong of the IFA test

[21] I find on a balance of probabilities that the agents of harm are not motivated to pursue the appellants to the IFAs and that this is determinative of their risks there. The appellants have not brought forward sufficient evidence to show that they are of interest to any authority outside of Punjab. The appeal submissions focus extensively on the means by which the appellants could be tracked elsewhere, from India's tenant verification system,24 to methods that police can use to track individuals through bank records and cellular phone signals,25 to India's national Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS) database,26 to the simple ability to ask after the appellants' whereabouts by questioning their family and friends in Punjab state.27 I accept that if the police are truly motivated to pursue an individual, then they have many means at their disposal to do so. What is determinative of these claims is that the police lack sufficient motivation to pursue the appellants in the IFAs, as was the case in Yuvraj Singh v. Canada.28 This decision is in line with Federal Court jurisprudence that, where an individual is at risk from local police in India, and they are not a high-profile individual, then, generally, an IFA is open to them.29 This would not require the appellants to live a life in hiding, or hide their whereabouts from their family.30

[29] The Gender Guidelines counsel that, while the threshold for demonstrating that relocation to an IFA is unreasonable is very high, Members should take an intersectional approach when considering whether this threshold has been met.39 When conducting this analysis, I have been guided by the following set of reasons published on the IRB website as "reasons of interest" which exemplify an intersectional approach to the assessment of risk of harm.40 When doing so and considering the situations of these appellants cumulatively, they have not established that the IFA locations would be unduly harsh for them.

[30] The objective documentary evidence indicates that large numbers of Sikh individuals are able to safely live in the IFA cities identified. The appellants would be relocating as a family unit that can support each other. The appellants do not submit that their XXXX health challenges leave them unable to work. The principal appellant testified that if he did not face problems with the police, he would anticipate being able to obtain work upon return to India. The principal appellant has significant education and work experience as an XXXX. The appellants have linguistic ability in English, which is widely spoken in the IFA locations. This is not a case in which the female appellants have testified that in the past they faced discrimination in India that amounted to persecution, setting aside the particular incidents considered in the first part of these reasons. It is also not a case in which the principal appellant's wife indicates that she continues to require any particular XXXX or other healthcare services to deal with her traumatic experiences in India. As the RPD observed, this appellant submitted evidence indicating that she sought such treatment about three years ago and she does not point to evidence on appeal indicating that she has required such services since.41 It appears from the medical report submitted by the XXXX in India that the appellant received considered and careful care where the medical professional not only had multiple meetings with that appellant, but also had conversations with other related individuals to ascertain relevant facts so as to best support this appellant. That appellant does not indicate in the appeal submissions that the care that she received was substandard or inadequate. In short, when considering the appellants' vulnerabilities as well as the circumstances which mitigate against a risk of harm, along with the objective country conditions, the appellants have not established that these IFA locations should rightfully be regarded as unreasonable ones that would more likely than not jeopardize their lives or safety.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION
[1] XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant), XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX (the associate appellants), citizens of India, appeal a decision rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

[2] The appellants state that they fear returning to India because they anticipate harm from police officers in their area of Punjab state who have raided their house and arrested and abused members of this family while alleging that they have links to gangsters and anti-national militants. The RPD rejected these claims, finding that the appellants had internal flight alternatives.
DETERMINATION

[3] I dismiss the appeals. The RPD was correct that the appellants have viable internal flight alternatives.
NEW EVIDENCE AND ORAL HEARING
The appellants' documents are all being considered

[4] On appeal, the appellants have applied to submit the following new documents:
(a) The Article "No Safe Haven: The Myth of the Internal Flight Alternative in India for Returned Sikh Asylum Seekers" by ENSAAF, dated December 27, 2004;
(b) A Comprehensive Discussion of the Internal Flight Alternative for Punjabi Sikh
Survivors of Political Rape and other Forms of Institutionalized Violence, by Judy Malik, Oct. 30, 2004; and
(c) The article "Internal Protection/Relocation/Flight Alternative as an Aspect of Refugee Status Determination," by James C. Hathaway and Michelle Foster.
[5] The first two documents are not admissible as new evidence because they were already submitted to the RPD and hence are on the record before me.

[6] The last document on Internal Protection/Relocation/Flight Alternative as an Aspect of Refugee Status Determination is admissible as a legal authority pursuant to RAD Rule 3(3)(f) because the appellants seek to rely on it for its propositions about how the Internal Flight Alternative legal test should be interpreted and applied.
[7] This Division cannot hold an oral hearing where it does not admit new evidence and is instead only considering additional legal authorities.1
ANALYSIS
[8] My role is to independently look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2

[9] In adjudicating these appeals, I am considering and applying the IRB Guideline on Gender Considerations3 and the Guideline on Child Refugee Claimants, which offer guidance with respect to gender- and child-specific issues present in these claims.4 I am also applying the Guideline on Procedures with Respect to Vulnerable Persons Appearing Before the IRB.5

[10] The Refugee Protection Division designated the principal appellant as a representative for the minor appellant. That designation continues at the RAD as per RAD Rule 23.
The RPD should have applied the gender guidelines, but this error is not determinative

[11] The RPD indicated that it applied the 1996 Guideline on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution. This was in error. In July 2022, the IRB Guideline on Gender Considerations replaced the previous 1996 Chairperson's Guideline on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.6 Members are expected to follow guidelines unless compelling or exceptional reasons exist to depart from them.7 The RPD was wrong not to consider and apply a guideline that had been in effect for well over a year at the time of this hearing and to instead apply a guideline that had been superseded.

[12] That said, this failure to refer to a guideline is not in itself a basis on which to overturn the decision. Instead, what matters is whether the RPD respected the guidelines in how it proceeded with the case at hand.8 Having reviewed the questioning and testimony at the hearing, I am satisfied that the RPD did not err in this respect.
INTERNAL FLIGHT ALTERNATIVE

[13] The appellants have viable IFAs in Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai, and Indore. As defined in Ranganathan v. Canada, an IFA is viable if 1) the appellants do not face s. 97 harm or a reasonable chance of persecution there, and 2) conditions in the IFA are such that it would not be unreasonable for the appellants to seek refuge there.9
First prong of the IFA test: Risk of persecution or s. 97 harm

[14] The appellants have not established on a balance of probabilities that the agents of harm are motivated to pursue them in the IFA locations such that they would face a reasonable chance of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, s. 97 harm there.
The agents of harm are not sufficiently motivated to pursue the appellants in the IFAs

[15] The RPD was correct that the appellants have not established that the police officers who are the agents of harm in this case are motivated to pursue them in the IFAs. While I accept that the police have visited the appellants' family and friends in their home state, and that this demonstrates that they have a continuing interest in the appellants, the appellants have not established that the police are motivated to take steps to track the appellants if they were residing in one of the IFAs elsewhere in the country.10 The primary reasons for reaching this conclusion are that it appears that police interest in the appellants has been extrajudicial and unofficial and that this is not the type of case in which police are motivated to cooperate in a multi-state manhunt.11 The objective documentary evidence indicates that police in different jurisdictions cooperate on major crimes.12 There is insufficient evidence before me that state police cooperate with police in other states to persecute individuals who have been pursued by local police and released upon payment of bribes without being charged with any crime.13

[16] This is not a case where the appellants have established that the police genuinely view them as militants or anti-nationals.14 Instead, the statements attributed to the authorities throughout the Basis of Claim narrative indicate that the agents of harm have accused the principal appellant of having information about militants from having worked at the same company as a suspected militant, or of having helped militants by, say, working with the family of a suspected one to make what the authorities described as a "false police complaint", but not of actually being a militant.15 As such, I conclude that the authorities are not motivated to pursue the appellants because they suspect them of being militant anti-nationals.

[17] In reaching this conclusion, I considered the appellants' argument that "in XXXX 2018 and XXXX 2018, the level of danger grew significantly for the appellants because of the court case they were planning to file against the police".16 They do not point to any specific evidence that the RPD ignored, for example evidence establishing that such a case was filed. When considering their risk as a result of such events, I place the most weight on the letter from the Indian lawyer who spoke with these appellants, who states that other people wanted to file a case, however this lawyer advised that they could only proceed with the case if the appellants offered to be witnesses, something that "they were unable to do".17 I am not satisfied that such discussions about a legal case mean that the agents of harm are motivated to pursue the appellants in the IFA locations.
It is not established that the agents of harm have pursued the appellants outside of Punjab

[18] Like the RPD, I find that the appellants have not credibly established on a balance of probabilities that the Punjab police have pursued them elsewhere in India. The appellants write in their narrative that the police did so, with the principal appellant stating that in XXXX 2019, police raided at Delhi for his wife because she had not reported to them, as expected. However, when the RPD asked questions about this alleged presence of the agents of harm in Delhi, in order to test the credibility of the allegation, the appellants offered shifting and inconsistent testimony. Specifically, a) at the hearing the principal appellant testified that there was a completely separate police raid in Delhi years prior that is not mentioned in the Basis of Claim narrative the appellants swore was complete, and b) the appellants provided inconsistent evidence about whether police raided their family member's home within four days of the principal appellant's arrival in 2017, causing him to flee at that point,18 or whether the principal appellant remained in that home for weeks19 and the police raid only occurred subsequent to his departure from India.20 These omissions and inconsistencies were not reasonably explained and, when asked to explain why their family member's affidavit does not mention multiple alleged police raids to his home, the principal appellant suggested that the family member lied or gave false evidence in the affidavit that the appellant provided to this Board.21

[19] The appellants do not dispute these credibility conclusions on appeal and I independently find that they are correct. The omission of the alleged police raid in Delhi is not reasonably explained as the appellants included less important events in their narrative, as the RPD noted. The appellants' testimony that they think that their family member may have given false evidence in the affidavit that they submitted to the Board does not reasonably explain the discrepancies identified by the RPD. Findings of credibility may be made on the basis that the witness failed to tender important evidence at an earlier opportunity, thus bringing into question whether it is a recent fabrication.22 Statements in support of a claim have to be accurate else the inaccuracies can be held against a claimant.23 The appellants do not submit that this evidence was affected by trauma or the other issues discussed in section 7 of this Board's gender guidelines.

[20] I conclude that the appellants' evidence about the agents of harm searching for them in Delhi is not credible and trustworthy. They have not established on a balance of probabilities that any such raids have occurred. That said, while I draw an adverse inference about the credibility of the appellants' evidence on this one point, this is not a case in which I conclude that the appellants are generally not credible or that their allegations regarding events in Punjab state are not credible.
Lack of motivation is determinative of the first prong of the IFA test

[21] I find on a balance of probabilities that the agents of harm are not motivated to pursue the appellants to the IFAs and that this is determinative of their risks there. The appellants have not brought forward sufficient evidence to show that they are of interest to any authority outside of Punjab. The appeal submissions focus extensively on the means by which the appellants could be tracked elsewhere, from India's tenant verification system,24 to methods that police can use to track individuals through bank records and cellular phone signals,25 to India's national Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS) database,26 to the simple ability to ask after the appellants' whereabouts by questioning their family and friends in Punjab state.27 I accept that if the police are truly motivated to pursue an individual, then they have many means at their disposal to do so. What is determinative of these claims is that the police lack sufficient motivation to pursue the appellants in the IFAs, as was the case in Yuvraj Singh v. Canada.28 This decision is in line with Federal Court jurisprudence that, where an individual is at risk from local police in India, and they are not a high-profile individual, then, generally, an IFA is open to them.29 This would not require the appellants to live a life in hiding, or hide their whereabouts from their family.30

[22] When reaching this conclusion, the RPD considered the 2004 report No Safe Haven: The Myth of the Internal Flight Alternative in India for Returned Sikh Asylum Seekers and the 2004 report A Comprehensive Discussion of the Internal Flight Option for Punjabi Sikh Survivors of Political Rape and other Forms of Institutionalized Violence. The appellants point to both reports again in their appeal submissions.31 The purpose of an appeal is not to merely re-argue a case, but instead to identify an error. The appellants have not done so in this respect. The RPD was correct to place limited weight on these documents, as they were written in 2004 and most of the information contained in them is based on incidents that occurred in the 1990s, when compared to the more current documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package.32

[23] This conclusion is also in line with UNHCR's guideline on internal relocation that the appellants point to, guidance which allows that an IFA may be viable in situations where an authority of the state has power that is limited to a specific geographical area.33
State protection is not at issue

[24] I reject the appellants' argument that "It is totally unreasonable to believe that there is any kind of state protection in the present situation."34 The determinative issue in this case is not whether the appellants could turn to a state mechanism related to the police misconduct at issue, but instead whether the appellants face a reasonable chance of encountering the harms that entitle an individual to protection in the IFAs given the motivation of the agents of harm.35
Canada's international obligations and the Canadian Charter of Rights are respected

[25] On appeal, the appellants submit that the RPD's decision does not respect Canada's international legal obligations, including the UN Convention against Torture and the principle of non-refoulement. They also submit that the RPD decision is in violation of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. RAD member Rouba Al-Salem responded to similar arguments in another case and I adopt her reasons as they apply to this case in front of me.36 International law and the Charter are not violated simply because this Board reaches a determination that is not favourable to the appellants.
Conclusion

[26] For the foregoing reasons, I find that the appellants do not face a reasonable chance of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, s. 97 harm in the IFAs.
Second prong of the IFA test: Jeopardy to life or safety in the IFA locations

[27] In order for an IFA to be viable, it must not be unduly harsh to expect an appellant to relocate to it. If there are conditions which would jeopardize the life or safety of the appellant in travelling to or temporarily relocating to the safe area, then it cannot be considered a viable IFA.37 In this case, the IFAs that the RPD proposed are reasonable ones.
Access to healthcare

[28] I accept that the principal appellant and his wife both have health conditions, but they have not established that their lives or safety would be imperiled by these health conditions in the IFAs as a result of an inability to access needed medical care. The appellants submit that access to healthcare in India can be limited for many individuals by its cost. I am not satisfied that these appellants would be unable to obtain needed healthcare because of its cost or unavailability. They submitted medical records indicating that in the past they were able to obtain healthcare while in India, including XXXX services and care from a doctor.38 They do not point to evidence in their appeal submissions arguing that the appellants were unable to obtain needed medical care while they were in India or that their medical needs have changed since. They have not satisfied me that upon return to India, it is more likely than not that they would no longer be able to obtain needed care.
Cumulative and intersectional assessment

[29] The Gender Guidelines counsel that, while the threshold for demonstrating that relocation to an IFA is unreasonable is very high, Members should take an intersectional approach when considering whether this threshold has been met.39 When conducting this analysis, I have been guided by the following set of reasons published on the IRB website as "reasons of interest" which exemplify an intersectional approach to the assessment of risk of harm.40 When doing so and considering the situations of these appellants cumulatively, they have not established that the IFA locations would be unduly harsh for them.

[30] The objective documentary evidence indicates that large numbers of Sikh individuals are able to safely live in the IFA cities identified. The appellants would be relocating as a family unit that can support each other. The appellants do not submit that their XXXX health challenges leave them unable to work. The principal appellant testified that if he did not face problems with the police, he would anticipate being able to obtain work upon return to India. The principal appellant has significant education and work experience as an XXXX. The appellants have linguistic ability in English, which is widely spoken in the IFA locations. This is not a case in which the female appellants have testified that in the past they faced discrimination in India that amounted to persecution, setting aside the particular incidents considered in the first part of these reasons. It is also not a case in which the principal appellant's wife indicates that she continues to require any particular XXXX or other healthcare services to deal with her traumatic experiences in India. As the RPD observed, this appellant submitted evidence indicating that she sought such treatment about three years ago and she does not point to evidence on appeal indicating that she has required such services since.41 It appears from the medical report submitted by the XXXX in India that the appellant received considered and careful care where the medical professional not only had multiple meetings with that appellant, but also had conversations with other related individuals to ascertain relevant facts so as to best support this appellant. That appellant does not indicate in the appeal submissions that the care that she received was substandard or inadequate. In short, when considering the appellants' vulnerabilities as well as the circumstances which mitigate against a risk of harm, along with the objective country conditions, the appellants have not established that these IFA locations should rightfully be regarded as unreasonable ones that would more likely than not jeopardize their lives or safety.
Conclusion

[31] I am therefore satisfied that the RPD properly applied both parts of the analysis as established in Rasaratnam, and correctly determined that the appellants have viable IFAs. The appellants have not shown that they face either a reasonable chance of persecution, or, on a balance of probabilities, s. 97 harm in the IFAs, or that it would be objectively unreasonable in their circumstances to relocate to these IFAs.
CONCLUSION

[32] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
